parakeet: Do you remember the first time you started to suspect that other believers were pretending? Maybe it was during a revival when someone slain in the spirit kept peeking to see if the moment was over. Maybe it was when you heard someone publicly testify about a miracle, only for them to privately admit their doubts. Or maybe it was much more personal. A moment when you realized that no matter how hard you prayed, no matter how much you tried to press into God's presence, you felt absolutely nothing. I had my suspicions for years, but one day I saw it so clearly I couldn't ignore it anymore. I was at a church service one time when the preacher declared, the glory of the Lord has filled this place. He said, I can't even see anymore. It's so thick in here. Suddenly, the first two rows of people started behaving like they had been blinded, hands reaching out, stumbling, acting like they couldn't see each other. But here's the thing the rest of us, all 500 of us sitting among them, we could see just fine, including some of the blinded people who had no trouble checking their text messages or making their way to the bathroom. That's when it really hit me. People will pretend if they find that it is socially required. And the real tragedy, even those who weren't directly participating were still enabling the illusion because nobody wanted to be the one to break character. And that's when I realized religious belief functions as a form of socially reinforced willful delusion, akin to an elaborate cosplay of psychosis. That may sound extreme, but let's unpack this. To start, faith is one big theatrical performance. Religious belief isn't just about believing, it's about performing belief. Cosplay isn't just costumes, it's a performance. In church, you don't just believe in God, you have to act like you believe in God. The worship service, the Holy Ghost dance, the way people fall out under the spirit, it's all interactive theater.
